What you have learned of Maresh, and the records you have found on the way.
What the islands believe, and what they have lived through.
The shores, roads and temples walked so far.
Words left in the world by other hands: notices, notes and inscriptions.

When a lamp goes out, it breaks into motes of light. Most of them lift toward the stars within a night and are gone. Some sink instead and drift seaward, cool and blue, and divers who meet that light underwater leave it be. The Order forbids binding glimmer into anything.

Once a generation a storm rises that does not move like weather. It wanders the sea as if it were looking for something, and it drowns whole coasts. For days afterward the water glows with the dead it leaves behind. The Order of the Still Water teaches that it is the price of the old binding, and that one day the price will be paid.

Each temple of the Order keeps a Saint: a Cantor of an earlier generation whose light stayed, the Order says, to teach the ones who come after. A Cantor who passes a temple's trial learns a verse of the Hush there and may call on its Saint from then on. The Shell Shrine's is Ilun, a great ray of netted light. When Asha calls him, the others step back and he stands in their place.

A fishing village in the Low Reaches, built of coral stone, with walls of set shells and roofs like opened fans. Carved gulls on the roof ridges watch the sea for weather. When the dead come in on the tide, its people go down to the beach to meet them, so that no one comes ashore alone.

A tidal road of saltgrass and coral boulders between Haluna and the Shell Shrine's islet. It opens this far only at the lowest tides, twice a month, on days the Order's tide-readers set. Reef crabs and lantern-lure eels keep to its pools, and old timber posts mark the line for anyone the turning tide catches.

Haluna's small temple of Water, on a tidal islet at the causeway's end. Its halls hold great shell-basins that turn to send the water where it is asked to go, until the inner pool fills and the chamber door floods open. It is tended and swept and loved, and it is the first temple on the road from Haluna.

A girl of Haluna who found Rhen in the shallows at dawn and smiled before she said a word. She woke her house before light that morning so the drowned would not come ashore alone, though no one had told her they were coming. The whole village treats her with a care that seems too gentle for an ordinary day.

Asha's guardian, who carries a long spear and the manners of a temple. He answers greetings with the Order's words before he has thought about them, and he weighs everything else he says as if it costs him. He watches Asha the way a man watches a lamp in the wind.

Nailed to a causeway post, the ink run by salt: "The road to the Shell Shrine stands open from the second hour after the low until the turn. Walk in company. Do not linger at the pools when the water begins to talk. If the tide takes the path, climb the nearest post and wait; the sea has always given this road back."

Cut into the first step of the shrine, worn smooth by knees: "Water does not hurry, and it is never late. Turn the shells gently and it will go where you ask. Leave the basins as you found them, for whoever comes after you."

Oruvel's divers go down weighted into the drowned towers of the Lit Age, with an oil lantern and a tether, and walk the floors instead of swimming them. They cut out old brass and glass and sell it by the pound to whoever pays, and the Order's scale-man stamps each lot unbound. Pockets of trapped air, the bell-rooms, let a diver breathe between floors. The oldest rule of the trade is that nobody goes below the ninth floor.
The Order of the Still Water

The faith of Maresh, whose sign is the Level: a circle crossed by one line of still water. It teaches that the Lit Age bound the dead and the sea rose to collect the debt, and that stillness is the atonement: build nothing that binds, keep no lamps but oil, mourn quietly and send the dead to the sea. Its people greet each other with "Be level" and answer "And still". Tenders keep its temples, and the Stillguard, in red-lacquered shell armour, keep its law.

The night before a Cantor leaves on pilgrimage, her village holds her funeral while she is alive to attend it. There is food, and there are songs, and her name is carved on a shell and set in the shrine wall beside the names of the Cantors who went before her. In Haluna the people carry their lamps out to the wall and leave their windows dark behind them.

A people descended from engineers who refused the Salt Edicts, and who wear the old insult in their name with pride. They live in flotillas of lashed hulls and put to work what the Lit Age bound, because, they say, the dead want to be useful. Each fine line tattooed on a wright's arm records a device the wright has restored. Their chalk sign, a circle with fine parallel lines, means that wrights work here, and the Order hunts them for it.

The drowned Lit Age towers under Oruvel, where the raft-town's lamp-divers work. The floors are coral-crusted concrete, and the galleries are rows of dead lamp-columns, white ceramic gone green, empty for four hundred years. Bell-rooms of trapped air hold a diver's breath between floors. A knotted cord across the stairwell says what every diver knows: nobody goes below the ninth floor.

A raft-town of lashed hulls in every colour the sun has faded, moored over a drowned Lit Age district in the Low Reaches. Its people are lamp-divers, poor and loud and fond of each other, and its plank bridges run between the scale-hull, the cookboats, the net lanes and the old keel-hull where the town meets. Carved gulls on every roof ridge face the sea; they are said to cry before the Undertow.

A two-masted Low Reaches ferry, hired by the Order to carry the Cantor from Haluna's islet to Pemakar for Lanternfall. She has a deckhouse with a small Order shrine, an awning for her passengers and a skiff on her davits. Her ferry-master, Imbe, keeps the old sea-law, and on this crossing she carries terrace traders, a Reed going home and a child too shy to look at the Cantor.

A terraced town on the flank of a volcano, its tiers cut into rice paddies, market terraces, smithies and lacquer workshops. Its gates are stone forearms with open hands, and its graves sit beside the paddies, so its festivals are held among the dead. At Lanternfall every household floats leaf-boats down the terrace channels until the whole mountain runs with small fires. The plume's thunder, they say, is Daro's hammer.

The temple of Lightning, a stair-mountain built into the lip of a caldera that still breathes ash. Old Lit Age copper veins its tiers, so the strikes run down the mountain like water down the terraces. Pilgrims climb past the Tenders' gate and the grave tier to a red-lacquered pavilion at the crown, where dry storms crackle in the plume.

Low water over a drowned country: grey-green silted flats, ridges of black Lit Age hull plating and wooden hulks, and tide-channels between them that fill faster than they look. Gulls work the wrecks at every hour. Saltwright chalk marks show where the wrights have been, and by law everything on the shoals is under the Edict.

A stilt city at a river mouth, with gilded lacquer signboards on every house-front, markets that float hull to hull, and a hundred languages. Above it hangs the Tamsule Bell, a dome of the Lit Age with a drop of seawater held in its mouth, lit from within. In Tidecup week the whole coast comes to watch the Reefball sides play, and every purse-cutter on the coast comes with it.

The stilt galleries inside the Bell's gantry, tier on tier around the catch-pool where the Tidecup is played. The drop hangs above them, perfectly still. Each side has its moorings under the Bell's skirt, iron rings set in a timber staging, and its people watch from the galleries over them.

A town that lives behind a seawall of grey laterite blocks carved with rows of faces, the Watchers, their eyes closed and their mouths open. The Fisher Stair is cut up the wall's inner face. The fishers of its stair-watch keep one law: first down the stair, last up it.

Oruvel's chandler, who has sold the lamp-divers their oil and trimmed their wicks for forty years from a hull she will not step off. She never learned to swim. She took Rhen in when he was eight and nobody came for him, the way she took in every stray the raft-town had, and she gives every diver a wick before they go down. "For luck."
Asha's aunt, who mends nets and pretends not to be afraid. She feeds Rhen the way you would feed a stray you have decided to keep: often, and far too much.

A scholar of Lamptongue from Ansedra, appointed by the Order to tutor the Cantor on her pilgrimage. She came aboard at the islet's landing with the Order's letter and very little else to say. She is exacting, correct and witheringly polite, and she keeps a step apart from everyone.

A silent, scarred swordsman who caught a child out of the weir at Pemakar and stayed with the party after. He says almost nothing, least of all about himself, and he swings a blade heavy enough to break armour.

A smith of Pemakar's forge lane, in his sixties, with burn-scarred forearms and a big, careful voice. He can true a blade to a hair and makes a ruin of folding a leaf-boat. His son went to Oruvel to learn to dive.

A Saltwright mechanic from the Hollowmere flotilla, quick and sharp with everyone. She was running a salvage camp on the Brine Shoals when the Order burned it, and she came away with one crate of parts and a grudge that could float a ship. Toma's Stillguard papers get her past the checkpoints, which is the reason she gives for staying.

The High Warden, head of the Order of the Still Water, met on the Brine Shoals on his once-a-Calm progress along the coast. His white barge leaves no wake. He is warm and witty, and humble in a way nobody on the coast expects of the head of their faith.

Mother Kell's grandson, captain of Oruvel's Reefball side in its oil-black and brass. He and Rhen grew up around the same stall on the second mooring. They are not brothers, but they had the same person.

A Kirru, far taller than a man, long-necked, with an otter's face and a crest of fine heron feathers. The name-shell at his throat has been scraped blank. He came down to the strand at Corrow on the night of the Ebbing, watched it a long while, and called it beautiful.

The temple of Fire, a hollow stone spire on the headland beyond Corrow's wall-gate, with copper flue-pipes coiled up its outside like vines. Its Tenders keep a flame that a Cantor must walk up the flues, tier by tier, to the crown. From the beacon gallery at the top you can see out to where the storms always break.

A Stillguard of Corrow's wall, Toma's shield-mate for seven years. He hugged Toma hard enough to lift him off the wall-head, knelt properly to the Cantor, and took to Rhen at once. Toma laughed out loud when he saw him.

A people of the estuaries, far taller than any human, with dark fur, a pale throat, an otter's face and a crest of heron feathers, who live some two hundred and fifty years. They speak softly and mean exactly what they say; among themselves they talk in whistle-clicks and hand-shapes. They live in clutches of brothers and sisters, led by the eldest who still swims, and each of them wears a name-shell at the throat. The Order tolerates them, has never tried to convert them, and keeps them out of its temples.

The people of the Ullar Heights, where the air is thin and the skies are enormous. They herd woolbacks on terraced valleys, weave a dense cloth, much of it, oddly, in tide patterns so far from the sea, and keep their records in keth, bundles of knotted cord read by touch. Up here the dead lift quickly, and the Ullari are calm about death in a way the coast finds cold.

Where the coast road from Corrow gives out, the land goes soft. Ossa Fen is a Kirru estuary of mangrove channels and tannin water, brown-black as steeped tea, and the only ways across it are the root-walks the Kirru keep between the trunks. White egrets stand in the shallows and do not startle. Something else lives in the roots.

A Kirru roost-village of woven reed lodges raised on mangrove roots round a still lagoon, reached by a causeway of reeds. Each lodge is a clutch's. The shore on its far side is where the clutches gather at dusk.

The largest Lit Age ruin still above water: stone galleries standing chest-deep in a turquoise lagoon, wrapped in strangler fig, their roofs the only dry way through. Ceramic conduits still run along the walls, and some of them still pulse faintly with bound light. Silent, gorgeous, and dead.

A temple of the Order half under water, built round the foot of a Lit Age well-shaft. Below the waterline its galleries are flooded, and in the sanctum at the bottom the deep's own cold wells up through the floor, carrying drowned glimmer down through it like silt. Nothing in it is frozen.

The road up into the Ullar Heights climbs a cliff in switchbacks, with cords strung post to post along the drop. These are the pass-cords. An Ullari who has lost someone ties a knot on them for the dead, and then walks on without looking back.

A highland town of stone and woven awnings on a terrace under the open sky: one street, an inn under a red banner, and a well in the square. Its walls are laid without mortar, many-sided stones fitted so close a blade would not go between them. The road north climbs on to Cloudloom.

A weaving-hall cut into the summit rock above Quellan, its roof open to the sky and hung with thousands of keth that stir in the thin wind. At noon the sun comes straight down through the roof, and the cords lay their shadows on the white stone floor like writing. It is stone and cord and sky, and a temple of the Order.

The holy city, the Order's seat, built on a lagoon kept perfectly flat. No wind ripples it and no wake is permitted; barges are poled, never rowed. Its skyline is bowl-domes, gilded and upturned on tiers of red lacquer, and the city has no seabirds, no dogs, and no games in its squares.

The Glimmer temple at the heart of Ansedra. Its inner basin is so still it is a perfect mirror, lit from beneath by a steady light that never moves, and the Order calls it a miracle: water that has not stirred in four hundred years. Pilgrims kneel at the ledge that rings it. Nobody walks on it.

The Order's library of Lit Age records, a long reading room between the stacks in Ansedra. The founders' lamp-ledgers and the full roll of the Cantors are kept here in plain sight, for anyone the Order lets in to read them.

The ceremonial heart of Ansedra: a stone floor on the still water under a red-lacquered colonnade, with galleries for guests, a dais for vows, and water-steps down to the moorings. A water-gate closes the canal beyond. The unions that matter to the faith are made here, before the Conclave of Elders.

The largest of the Saltwright flotillas: a raft-city of some four thousand people on lashed hulls, turning windmills and tide-wheels, that moves with the seasons among the outer shoals to keep ahead of the Order's patrols. No chief rules it; a council of hull-captains does. Its people find their way by current-songs.

The southern edge of the known sea. For days of wading the water runs ankle to waist deep over white sand, the horizon goes white and the sky with it, and there is nothing to steer by but the cairns the waders keep.
A ring of colossal stone figures standing in the water round a sunken amphitheatre, their mouths open. Those who know of it say it is where every Cantor ends.

The years between one Undertow and the next. The Order counts them from the Level, and the coast lives by that count: this is the year 1012, at the end of the sixty-first Calm. Calms used to last a lifetime. This one has lasted eleven years.

When a Calm begins to fail, the Order names a Cantor to sing the next one. She walks a pilgrim's road from temple to temple with a tutor in Lamptongue and a sworn guardian, and with anyone else she chooses to take, learning a verse of the Hush at each. At the road's end she sings the Hush whole, and the storm sleeps. Her village holds her funeral before she leaves, and no one says why.

The Order's dance for the dead. After a drowning a priest dances on a floating platform with a long lantern-staff, and the motes of the dead follow the staff out to sea while the mourners kneel facing the water. After an Undertow the dance falls to a Cantor, and the whole strand watches her. It is the most beautiful thing the Order does.

An Inquisitor of the Stillguard, one of the officers who enforce the Salt Edicts, met on the Brine Shoals with a raid-hound and a long-hafted brine-iron. He is in his forties, tired, and sincere: he believes in what he burns. When the fight was done he knelt in the mud, and when the High Warden told him to put the iron in the water, he did not argue.

When a Kirru dies, the clutch gathers at the tideline at dusk and sings the farewell-tide, a wordless song that rises and keeps rising. Then they turn their backs to the water, so that the dead are not held by being watched. Within the hour the light goes up, straight up, and no one turns to see it go.

Every Kirru wears a shell at the throat with their name cut into it, a spiral of notches no human script can read. It is not a keepsake: the Kirru keep nothing of their dead, and the shell is the name itself. A shell ground blank means its wearer has been sent away, until they can sing for the one they would not let go.

A clutch is led by the eldest who still swims, and at Reedhollow that is a Kirru older than the lagoon's oldest roots. The eldest speaks the human tongue slowly, as if each word were borrowed and had to be given back. Pell is not let past the fen's edge.

The eldest of Reedhollow's clutch who still swims: grey at the muzzle, her crest gone white. She lets strangers into the village for what they have done, and keeps out the one who walked them there, because he did not turn around.

Liss's older brother, a Hollowmere wright with a loud laugh in a quiet city. When the Order asked the flotilla for a groom for a Warden's daughter, he volunteered, so that nobody would have to be chosen.
A Warden's daughter of Ansedra, who chose a Saltwright and learned his knots. Brave in a city that is never loud.

The fifty-sixth Cantor, the only Kirru ever named, and Pell's clutch-sister. She heard the dead, and believed she could end the storm from inside it. The Order keeps her as the Saint the pilgrims call Nhoa.

The forty-seventh Cantor, an Ullari keth-reader who started counting on her pilgrimage. She tied the count into cords and hung it in Cloudloom among thousands, where nobody thought to read it. Then she sang anyway.

The sixtieth Cantor: a Tender of Ansedra, patient, funny, and a terrible cook. Ysolde's husband. The Order raised him to the Sanctum as the Saint Ethren, and she has visited him every year for twenty-four years.
A Warden of the Conclave of Elders, with a soldier's bearing and a magistrate's voice. He read the decree at the peace wedding, and came after the bridal barge across the lagoon.
The five who stand above the Wardens: the High Warden and four more, veiled at every rite. They speak rarely, and the Order obeys them without asking why.
A Stillguard commander, grey-bearded and decent, who taught a Haluna fisher's son to hold a shield. At the peace wedding he ordered that son to stand aside.
Hollowmere's dock-master, keeper of the flotilla's dry-dock berths, father of Liss and Tobin. Grief in his house is work and bowls set out without asking.
The first Cantor, a Lamplighter of Iskarra, who sang herself into the storm a thousand years ago. She has been awake in the Choir's stones ever since.

Kerrid kept the Fisher Stair at Corrow for fourteen years, captain of a watch of conscripted fishers, with no rank in the Order. In 1001 he held the stair for a Cantor and a diver who had never met, and the sea took him off the bottom step. His light did not lift. He is one of the unrisen: held, and still keeping the watch, because somebody is still below.

The Ullari write with cord. A keth is a bundle of knotted strings, and the kind of each knot, its place on the string and the string's colour carry a word, a number or a name; a reader runs the fingers along it, and a good one can read in the dark. Herds, debts, weddings and the dead are all kept the same way. The cords on the passes are keth too, and every knot there is a name.

The Order's words for those it puts out of the faith. No Order shrine will answer them and no Order keeper will trade with them, nobody of the faith may answer their "Be level", and the Stillguard may take them wherever the Order's word runs. At the Lacquer Court the party was declared outside the Level for sheltering binders. The Kirru and the Saltwrights keep shrines of their own, and those still answer.

The storm is the dead who were never let go, and it wants to come apart. The Hush does not put it to sleep. It gives the storm a heart to hold on to, and the heart is the Cantor who sings it. Every Cantor since the first has ended there.
